name: Christmas Tree Un-decoration
description: Figure D.1: Christmas tree. Last Christmas, you had a lovely Christmas tree with $$$n$$$ vertices, numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ and rooted at vertex $$$1$$$. For each $$$i$$$ ($$$2 \le i \le n$$$), vertex $$$p_i$$$ is the parent of vertex $$$i$$$. The tree is decorated beautifully with $$$a_i$$$ ornaments on vertex $$$i$$$ ($$$1 \le i \le n$$$). However, it has already been a few months since Christmas, and it is time to take down all the ornaments and put your tree away until next year. Since this process is tedious, you have decided to make it more fun by using only the following operation, which you can perform zero or more times: Choose a vertex $$$u$$$. For each vertex $$$v$$$ on the unique simple path from vertex $$$1$$$ to vertex $$$u$$$ (inclusive), remove exactly one ornament from $$$v$$$ if there is any left. While you are still determining the minimum number of operations needed, your little child modifies the number of ornaments on the tree. More precisely, your child makes $$$q$$$ changes. In the $$$j$$$-th change, the number of ornaments on vertex $$$u_j$$$ is modified to $$$x_j$$$ ($$$1 \le j \le q$$$). Note that these changes are persistent; the effect of each change carries over to subsequent changes. Note that you do not actually perform any operations on the tree. For the initial configuration and after each change, your task is to determine the minimum number of operations needed to remove all the ornaments from the tree at each moment.
input_specification: The first line of input contains one integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10\,000$$$) representing the number of test cases. After that, $$$t$$$ test cases follow. Each of them is presented as follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$q$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 200\,000$$$; $$$1 \le q \le 200\,000$$$). The second line contains $$$n-1$$$ integers $$$p_2, p_3, \ldots, p_n$$$ ($$$1 \le p_i \lt i$$$ for all $$$2 \le i \le n$$$). The third line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \le 10^9$$$ for all $$$1 \le i \le n$$$). The $$$j$$$-th of the next $$$q$$$ lines contains two integers $$$u_j$$$ and $$$x_j$$$ ($$$1 \le u_j \le n$$$; $$$1 \le x_j \le 10^9$$$). The sum of $$$n$$$ across all test cases in one input file does not exceed $$$200\,000$$$. The sum of $$$q$$$ across all test cases in one input file does not exceed $$$200\,000$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output $$$q+1$$$ lines. The first line should contain the minimum number of operations required for the initial tree. The $$$j$$$-th of the following $$$q$$$ lines should contain the minimum number of operations required after the $$$j$$$-th change happens.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2206D — Christmas Tree Un-decoration [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
